question: In 2021, we welcomed Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan. This created momentum for action, which needs to be sustained. Some cancers are better known than others, and some require extra care and attention, including from policymakers. Pancreatic cancer is one of the most lethal forms of cancer and is the fourth largest cause of cancer death in Europe.

Despite its significant public health impact, effective treatments exist only for early cancers, where complete surgical resection is possible. There are not enough high-profile research efforts to improve care. Pancreatic cancer has the lowest rate of survival of all cancers across Europe, killing about 92 % of patients within five years of diagnosis.

When diagnosed, 80 % of patients already have tumours that are at too late a stage to be cured. The five-year survival rate for pancreatic cancer is below 8 %. European funding can provide desperately needed advances in this area. 1.
What steps is the Commission undertaking to support effective approaches to and treatment of pancreatic cancer?
How is the Commission planning to ensure that an appropriate level of funding and support is maintained for pancreatic cancer research and care?
answer: In Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan (1), the Commission has included actions, which address cancers with poor prognosis, including pancreatic cancer. These include support to Member States to establish and expand Comprehensive Cancer Centres and Networks, complemented by an EU-wide network, and specifically the establishment of several new networks of expertise addressing, amongst others, complex cancers.

With regard to the latter, the Commission awarded a Direct Grant to the Member States’ authorities under the 2021 EU4Health Work Programme (2) leading to the establishment in 2022 of the Joint Action on new (cancer) Networks of Expertise (JANE (3)). The aim is to increase the survival rate of cancer patients with poor prognosis above 33%.

Existing models and initiatives on pancreatic cancer were evaluated and mapped. Domains defined for work on pancreatic cancer include: 1) clinical care; 2) research and innovation; 3) education and training; and 4) policy and patient engagement.

This work will continue in a follow-up Joint Action (JANE 2) funded under the 2023 EU4Health Work Programme with the aim to create an EU Network of Expertise on pancreatic tumours. Horizon Europe (4) has provided and will continue to provide opportunities for research and innovation on cancer (5), including on unmet needs of patients with pancreatic cancer.
For example, in the context of the EU Cancer Mission there have been calls addressing risk factors (6), clinical studies in patients with refractory cancers (7), and immunotherapy (8).

Horizon Europe Cluster 1-Health has addressed better care for cancer patients through artificial intelligence and machine learning (9) and the European public-private partnership Innovative Health Initiative (10) has addressed personalised, multimodal cancer therapies (11).
